title: Antonelli surges to dominant victory in United States GP
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli kept his composure to triumph at the United States Grand Prix and take another step towards clinching the Drivers’ Championship, edging out Charles Leclerc and Max Verstappen in a strategic race.

The Italian’s superb opening lap combined with Verstappen’s poor start to give him an early lead, which he held onto through an inspired one-stop strategy to secure his ninth Grand Prix victory of the season.

While many of his rivals stopped twice, Antonelli delivered a mighty stint on the medium tyres before managing the hard compound all the way to the chequered flag, eking out a margin of 13.078s even after a Virtual Safety Car slowed the field before the final lap.

Behind him, a late move promoted Leclerc to a second consecutive P2 finish as Verstappen withstood multiple niggles with his Red Bull to complete the podium, with Lewis Hamilton adding to Ferrari’s points haul in fourth place.

Lando Norris saw his opportunity of a podium disappear with his ageing tyres, leaving him in P5 ahead of Red Bull’s Isack Hadjar and the second McLaren of Oscar Piastri.

A frustrating day for George Russell saw him wind up in eighth place, followed by Liam Lawson and Pierre Gasly in the last of the points-paying positions. Nico Hulkenberg, Arvid Lindblad and Gabriel Bortoleto missed out as they took P11 to P13, with the Brazilian bouncing back from a substantial 80-place grid penalty.

Esteban Ocon took P14 from the Aston Martin pair of Lance Stroll and Fernando Alonso as Haas failed to score in their home race.

In similarly bad news for Williams, they extended their point-less streak to three events as Alex Albon and Carlos Sainz led Sergio Perez in rounding out the finishers in Austin.

There were three retirements for Alpine’s Franco Colapinto, Haas’ Ollie Bearman and Cadillac’s Valtteri Bottas, with the latter pulling to the side of the track to cause the VSC that neutralised some of the last laps.

AS IT HAPPENED

The first two days of action at the Circuit of The Americas had produced plenty of challenges as well as another close contest between the top teams, but Sunday was time for the paddock to shift their focus to the main event.

While Ferrari had set the pace throughout Free Practice, and McLaren and Red Bull both looked competitive in Qualifying, it was Drivers’ Championship leader Antonelli who had sealed pole position with what Toto Wolff described as “a miracle lap”.

It put the Italian within touching distance of his maiden title, but that would rely on three things – victory in the 56-lap Grand Prix while Russell placed ninth or below, and Hamilton finished outside of the top four.

Such a result was certainly possible after the Britons qualified P6 and P5 respectively, but it remained to be seen whether Antonelli would be able to hold off the impressive Red Bull pair at lights out, with Verstappen targeting a third consecutive win.

Ahead of the race, a number of changes to the order were confirmed. Lindblad would line up in P14 as Colapinto and Bortoleto dropped to P20 and P21, all three having exceeded the allocation for various power unit components.

In addition, Aston Martin’s Stroll was required to start from the pit lane after his car was modified under Parc Ferme conditions and additional PU elements were used, sacrificing his P18 finish in Qualifying.

Once all 22 cars were in position and the tyre blankets were removed, it was revealed that the field was divided over tyre compounds, with the Mercedes and McLaren drivers set to begin on the mediums as the rest of the top 10 – including the Red Bulls – bolted on the softs.

Nearly everyone else had also opted for the grippier rubber, apart from Bottas and Colapinto on the hards, and Stroll on the mediums.

After the formation lap was completed without any drama, the five red lights went out to kick off the United States Grand Prix, and a great launch from Antonelli saw him hold onto the lead whilst Verstappen fell into the clutches of the Ferrari pair.

Leclerc executed a confident overtake to improve to P2, with the Dutchman seemingly suffering a deployment issue, and Hamilton went side-by-side but ultimately settled for P4. However, before the first lap had ended, Verstappen found the performance he needed to reclaim second place and set his sights on Antonelli.

Although a short Virtual Safety Car period followed to recover some debris from the track, it didn’t last long enough for Verstappen to make a significant dent in Antonelli’s lead, with the Italian enjoying a 2s advantage at the front of the field.

Elsewhere, Hadjar had dropped back to P5 as the major winners and losers from the opening laps were revealed – Bearman, Ocon and Albon had all gained three positions each whilst Hulkenberg and Alonso lost a handful of places further down the order.

Albon’s progress came at the cost of earlier contact with Alonso, who was putting pressure on Sainz in his ambition to move into P16, which he achieved five laps into the race. Replays also showed that the latter had been squeezed into the pit wall in the Williams, and Bearman had also bumped into Gasly.

Back in the top 10, it was announced that Russell was under investigation for leaving the track and gaining an advantage after banging wheels with Piastri’s McLaren. Upon learning of this, the Briton insisted: “I was on the inside, he was overtaking on the outside. That’s his risk.”

Nevertheless, the stewards ruled that a five-second time penalty was deserved – good news for Norris, who was steadily closing the gap to sixth-placed Russell after McLaren had switched him with Piastri.

By Lap 10, Antonelli had built a margin of nearly 3s over Verstappen, but plenty of action was unfolding outside of the points. A back-and-forth battle saw Alonso get back past Albon for P15, and Colapinto was similarly trying to challenge Sainz further behind.

Team orders were imposed for a second time in the race when Haas told their drivers to swap positions, Bearman having shared concerns about his car’s strange handling. They therefore chose to prioritise Ocon’s undamaged machine in the hope of breaking into the points at their home event, with the Frenchman shuffling up to P11.

That was soon validated as Bearman continued to drop down the order before following Verstappen into the pits on Lap 14 – the Dutchman was given another set of soft tyres and emerged in eighth place, crucially making the most of the clear air to quickly close in on Piastri.

Hamilton was the next to peel off for a pit stop and was soon joined by Leclerc and the Australian, theoretically locking in a two-stop strategy for Ferrari and McLaren, with Norris changing his tyres a lap later.

Contrastingly, Mercedes relied on the medium compound to extend their first stint, but it didn’t take long for Verstappen to pass Russell and get back into the top three behind his team mate Hadjar, who said that his tyres felt “okay” and suggested that he “should stay out for a bit”.

Bearman’s tough day went from bad to worse as he was handed a 10-second time penalty whilst running in P18, effectively ruling out any chance of scoring points as he responded “are you kidding me?” to news of the decision – he later retired with damage.

Meanwhile, Antonelli was making the most of a 12s buffer over Hadjar as his engineer told him to “go as long as we can”, confirming that a one-stop was the likely approach for the Silver Arrows over the remaining laps.

They did, however, call Russell in to serve his penalty and take on the hard compound, which dropped him to P10 just as Hadjar was ordered to let his faster team mate past, which he obeyed after some initial resistance.

Verstappen was therefore freed to chase down Antonelli, but his mission was made much easier by the Italian stopping for fresh tyres at the end of Lap 24.

He returned to the circuit in fourth place, narrowly staying ahead of Hamilton before attention moved onto a tight contest for P3 between Leclerc and Hadjar, which was cut short again when Hadjar finally got rid of his softs.

Red Bull’s recovery from their shaky start was jeopardised by issues for both of their drivers, with the Frenchman apparently stuck on incorrect mapping that impacted the throttle, and Verstappen fighting an “undriveable” car.

When asked for an update on his front wing, he stated that he had “literally no idea”, so with Ferrari’s Leclerc creeping ever closer Red Bull brought him in for his second stop. Unfortunately for the Monegasque, his inherited lead was brief as Antonelli charged past to recapture his original starting position.

That left him in first place ahead of Leclerc and Hamilton with 20 laps to go, but he did have a tense moment with backmarker Sainz – the Spaniard didn’t get out of the way quickly enough, forcing Antonelli into a lock-up at Turn 12.

It didn’t appear to unnerve him too much as he continued to pump in strong laps whilst the Ferraris pitted again, promoting Norris and Verstappen to the podium spots as McLaren advised their driver to stay out on his hard tyres.

Although that may have been their best opportunity to finish on the rostrum, Verstappen quickly cut his deficit down to less than a second and sailed past at the beginning of Lap 47, commanding a three-way battle for P2 as Leclerc sought to demote Norris further.

Despite a lock-up, the Monegasque thrived in the tantalising battle and swept past the McLaren driver, who was evidently struggling to nurse his tyres more and more as the laps ticked down.

Leclerc wasn’t done attacking quite yet and overtook Verstappen for P2 – possibly aided by engine braking troubles on the RB22 – as his team mate similarly stormed past Norris to move into fourth place.

The race was neutralised when Bottas slowed and pulled to the side of the track, causing a Virtual Safety Car to be deployed while the marshals moved his Cadillac to a safer place, but such was Antonelli’s lead at this stage that it put minimal pressure on him.

Normal conditions resumed with a few laps to go and the Italian continued to control from the front, remaining there all the way to the chequered flag as Leclerc settled for second place just over 13s behind.

Verstappen finished on the podium for a sixth event in a row, denying Hamilton and Norris as Hadjar took P6 in the second Red Bull. Nearly 18s further back, Piastri settled for seventh ahead of Russell, Lawson and Gasly.

Audi missed out on the points with Hulkenberg taking P11, followed by Lindblad, Bortoleto and Ocon in a tricky day for the midfield outfits. The Aston Martins of Stroll and Alonso were next in the order with Albon, Sainz and Perez rounding out the finishers after earlier retirements for Bottas, Colapinto and Bearman.

Key quote

"It was the result we needed," said Antonelli. "The whole team deserve it so much and all this time putting in so much work on bringing this new package and finally seeing the result is very pleasant and it was also perfect execution from strategy to call the one-stop so I’m really happy we made it stick and it was a great team effort."

What's next

title: Gademan grabs second win with assured Austin drive
excerpt:
Nina Gademan converted her third-place start into her second race win of the season in the F1 ACADEMY Feature Race in Austin, overtaking Emma Felbermayr to take second in the drivers’ standings with two races to go.

The Alpine driver took control at the first corner, overtaking both Payton Westcott and newly crowned 2026 F1 ACADEMY champion Alisha Palmowski around the outside of Turn 1. Gademan put clean air between herself and the rest of the field, executed a perfect Safety Car restart, and held firm for her second win of the campaign.

An unfortunate collision between Palmowski and Alba Larsen forced both drivers to retire from second and third place. This allowed Westcott to take a podium on home soil, finishing in P2, while Natalia Granada rounded out the top three with her first podium since Shanghai.

Jade Jacquet found herself under pressure from Emma Felbermayr for the majority of the race. Still, the Williams driver held on to fourth, her best finish of the season so far, while the Audi driver settled for fifth.

Lisa Billard and Rachel Robertson finished P6 and P7, while Ella Lloyd charged from 13th to eighth to gain valuable points. Esmee Kosterman overtook two cars on the final lap to take ninth, while Megan Bruce took the final point, making it a double-points-scoring weekend for the TAG Heuer driver.

F1 ACADEMY heads back to the bright lights of Las Vegas, as the 2026 season draws to a close with Round 6 from November 19-21.

title: Why Alonso seems as hungry as ever 20 years on from his last title
excerpt:
Many years ago, Graham Hill’s friends and admirers privately worried when he insisted on carrying on as an F1 driver going into the 1973 season.

He had proved himself time and time again to be a very quick driver who could get the job done. Back in 1962 he had emerged as Jim Clark’s strongest rival and won that year’s World Championship.

Poignantly, he did it again in 1968, carrying the shattered Lotus team on his shoulders after the Scot’s death that April.

title: How Lawson helped Lindblad by sacrificing his Q3 run
excerpt:
Grid penalties can often lead to different strategies in Formula 1 Qualifying. Typically if they are destined to start at the back the drivers concerned only make a token effort in Q1, and either don’t appear later in the session, or perhaps switch to helping their team mate with a tow – as was the case with Gabriel Bortoleto and his Audi partner Nico Hulkenberg in Austin.

Teams also always have to avoid tricky situations where, for example, a penalised driver bumps his unpenalised team mate down the order so that he doesn’t progress to the next session.

Saturday’s United States Grand Prix Qualifying saw an unusual take on the theme. A driver who had made the top 10 in Q2 and didn’t have a grid penalty was kept in the garage during Q3 in order to help his team mate – who did have a penalty.

This was the story that unfolded at Racing Bulls after Arvid Lindblad came into the weekend with a five-place drop for taking a new ICE.

The VCARB 03 had enough pace to head the midfield pack, and thus Lindblad and his team mate Liam Lawson were both able to make it to Q3.

Given that the cars ahead of them were the eight from the four top teams, and there were no Audis or Alpines in the mix, they were always destined to finish the final session in P9 and P10.

And in order to ensure that Lindblad got the higher position, which would convert to P14 on the final grid, the decision was made to not allow Lawson to run in Q3 – something that naturally went against his racer’s instincts.

He was thus classified P10 with no time achieved, but he will start a place ahead after Lindblad drops down the order.

"I would have loved to have a go at Q3,” said the New Zealander. “We actually got there with two sets as well, which is not normal for us. In a normal situation, if we're fighting an Alpine or an Audi, having those two sets would have been great to use.

“I would have loved to have a go at it, but considering Arvid's got a penalty, we were going to be ninth and 10th anyway, it just doesn't really make sense. Now we have plenty of tyres for tomorrow.”

Lindblad, Colapinto and Bortoleto penalised for US GP

Lawson admitted that it wasn’t easy to climb out of the cockpit and watch his team mate head out of the garage. “I asked to go out, to be honest," he added. "I said I want to go and do it, and they said no. So yeah, it's frustrating a little bit for a driver, especially because we've had a very strong weekend so far.

“The car's been very good. Q1 on one set, we were comfortably through. Q2 was a little bit more tricky to be honest. But going to Q3 with two sets of tyres would have would have been lots of fun.”

Crucially, given the battle for P5 in the Constructors' Championship, Lawson starts immediately ahead of Alpine’s Pierre Gasly.

“To be fair, it was very, very close with Pierre in Q2,” he said. “But obviously we're one set less at that point. We were ready to go if we needed to in Q3 there. The car's been good in the long run as well. So hopefully tomorrow we can have a good race.”

Lindblad meanwhile was pleased with how the session turned out, although he too was compromised in that he only did one run in Q3 when he had the tyres available for a second.

“I think it makes sense what we did,” he said. “For sure, I would have loved to have another go. We both had an extra set left, and we were close I think to P8 in Q2, but realistically, the top teams always pull another gear when we get to Q3.

“So realistically, we would have both been in the same position we are now – maybe gone half a second or six-tenths quicker. But I was happy with Q2.”

Heading the midfield pack is always an achievement, so was there some frustration at not being able to start from the P9 he originally earned?

“Yeah, I guess so,” he said. “But at the same time I knew coming into the weekend I would take the penalty. I mean, it's a bit of a shame that it was only two races ago I was taking a penalty already, but it is what it is. That's just the nature of how things are with the new engines this year.

“But very happy with today. It's not been an easy week. I've been slower than Liam in every session so far – I think eight or nine-tenths slower than him in the first run of Q1. So to be ahead at the end of Q2 when it mattered, I'm obviously very happy with.

“But at the same time, looking ahead to tomorrow now because that's where the points are scored, I think on this track, overtaking is possible. So just being with a good pace will help us to come through.”

title: ‘We can’t fix core problems' – Albon on Williams' Qualifying
excerpt:
Alex Albon conceded Williams were struggling to "fix core problems" as the team's struggles at the United States Grand Prix weekend continued with another disappointing day.

After finishing bottom of the timesheets in both FP1 and FP2, the Thai driver made some improvement in FP3 by finishing ahead of team mate Carlos Sainz and the Cadillac pairing of Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas, but remained almost 2.8 seconds off the pace of Lewis Hamilton at the front.

Things did not get any better for Williams though in Saturday's Qualifying session, with both drivers eliminated in Q1 after struggling to keep the car on track at the Circuit of The Americas.

Sainz, who admitted on Friday that he “wasn’t expecting any miracles” across this United States Grand Prix weekend, will start in P17 on Sunday, while Albon will line-up one place behind him in P18 as the pair were elevated two spots thanks to the grid penalties for Franco Colapinto and Gabriel Bortoleto.

When asked for his instant reaction to Saturday’s Qualifying runs, a confused Albon admitted: “Maybe we need to review our run plan a bit. I felt like we went out really early on the last run.

“We’ve been fighting a lot with the car, with the tyres. Honestly, I finished Qualifying just as confused as I was in FP1. We were trying everything. We’re doing different set-ups every session and yet we can’t fix core problems in the car.

“We throw stuff at the wall – spaghetti at the wall, I guess – and hope that it sticks, but nothing sticks. Let’s see tomorrow.”

The frustration is clear inside the Williams garage, although the disappointing results in Austin have been partly blamed on the ongoing tests taking place as they look further ahead towards the 2027 season.

Speaking after Qualifying, Sainz explained: “It’s been a general weekend where we’ve invested a lot into next year and probably didn’t maximise the car until the last laps of Qualifying. I did some really good laps and we changed a few things on the set-up that helped me be a bit more comfortable today, especially in that Qualifying session.

“On that last lap I was probably just pushing too hard. I did a mega Sector 1, mega Sector 2 and unfortunately I couldn’t close the lap. Maybe with a perfect Sector 3 we could’ve put it in towards the top end of Q1 or even Q2, but I’ll take it.

“I think we’ve been brave with the set-up and testing a few things. I was quite brave on that lap, but unfortunately I did a mistake towards the end and I couldn’t close it.

"We’re definitely learning a few things about next year. We are investing a lot in it, but it’s also true that we cannot hide the fact that we have a very poor car at a track like Austin.

“Not even with investing all that time developing all those things for next year, we would be any better today. We are slow – it’s what it is. We’re trying our best, but until the end of the year I don’t expect any miracles.”

title: Toto Wolff reveals sneaky office chat with Kimi Antonelli ahead of USGP victory
excerpt:
Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff has revealed that Kimi Antonelli sneaked into his office ahead of winning the United States Grand Prix to tell him he did not feel any nerves about the world title.

Antonelli has moved to the brink of becoming Formula 1's youngest world champion after a dominant win from pole position at the Circuit of the Americas.

It represented his first victory since the Spanish Grand Prix and one that has made it all but a formality that he will become world champion in Mexico City.

The 20-year-old made an excellent start and kept the lead into the first corner before committing to a one-stop strategy, while those around him all chose a two-stop.

He remained calm and near-perfect throughout the race and only exceeded track limits once, in a drive that left Wolff incredibly proud.

Asked how proud he is of Antonelli, Wolff told Sky F1: "Yeah, what a boy, no? I was just saying before, I got a question about whether he was nervous before the race, and I said, ‘Oh, he just sneaked into my office before getting ready and said, 'I'm just going to enjoy this right now, and it's weird, I'm not thinking about the championship at all. Isn't that funny?'

"So he's on a discovery mission there, also in terms of what's happening to him emotionally, and then he just delivered from the beginning to the end. It was exceptional at any time."

Mercedes reap reward of one-stop confidence

Mercedes very much stuck to its guns when it came to Antonelli's strategy, despite Max Verstappen, who was running second early in the race, having committed to a two-stop strategy very early on.

The Silver Arrows did not blink, with a one-stop strategy turning out to be the quickest option, switching from the medium compound to the hards.

"Yeah, strategy has really done a good job today," added Wolff. "We discussed the possibility that Max could undercut us, and we stayed firm with the decision, saying the one-stop looks like the fastest strategy.

"Norris hit the hards and looked very good, so we stayed solid. And at the end, it came out pretty much as expected. In theory, it was eight seconds quicker, and at the end, it was a little bit more."

title: Max Verstappen questions Red Bull strategy in third consecutive victory failure
excerpt:
Max Verstappen questioned whether Red Bull's strategy left the team with the right tyres available after failing to secure a third consecutive victory.

The four-time world champion started on the front row in second but was slow off the line, making a dive on Kimi Antonelli at the first corner impossible.

Verstappen was overtaken by Charles Leclerc in the opening corners but quickly reclaimed the position at the end of the first lap before settling into the race.

Red Bull quickly committed to a two-stop strategy, although the Dutchman's second stint saw him complain and describe his RB22 as "undriveable".

Verstappen's first two stints were on the softs before he moved onto the mediums, where his pace improved, allowing him to move through the field and back into second.

Unfortunately, the 29-year-old was overtaken by Leclerc in the closing laps, leaving him to finish third behind the Ferrari driver and race winner Antonelli. Had it not been for a very late Virtual Safety Car, Lewis Hamilton may also have passed the Red Bull.

The Red Bull star acknowledged that he had got fortunate towards the end, but said the greater problem was the tyres at his disposal.

"I think our overall pace was not good enough, and then probably also the tyres that we had available were probably not the right ones," said Verstappen.

"So, that’s something that we have to understand, because the last few races it was always working well for us.

"For whatever reason it didn’t work out here, but we still managed to get on the podium. Maybe a little bit lucky with the VSC at the end, but I’ll take it."

title: Kimi Antonelli 'very close' to F1 history after 'perfect execution'
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli hailed the "perfect execution" of his Mercedes team's race strategy for leaving him "very close" to becoming the youngest F1 drivers' champion in the sport's history.

From pole position at the Circuit of the Americas, Antonelli was never troubled en route to taking the United States Grand Prix chequered flag for his ninth win overall of a scintillating campaign.

With five races remaining, Antonelli now leads Mercedes team-mate George Russell by 123 points, and Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton by 124 points, meaning he needs to finish ninth or higher next weekend in Mexico City to take the title, if Russell wins.

Following a consummate performance at COTA to underline his stunning season, Antonelli said: "It was the result we needed, and the whole team deserve it so much.

"All this time putting so much work into bringing this new package and finally seeing the result is very pleasant.

"It was also a perfect execution from strategy to call the one-stop, and I'm really happy that we made it stick, and today was a great team effort."

With one hand on the F1 drivers' trophy now, he added: "Yeah, we're very close. We'll try to finish on a high, and hopefully we can clinch it very soon."

title: How Kimi Antonelli can win the F1 title in Mexican Grand Prix
excerpt:
How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico City

Kimi Antonelli must wait until at least the Mexico City Grand Prix to be crowned as F1 world champion after missing out in the United States.

The Mercedes driver could have won the title in Austin if he had won the race, George Russell had finished ninth or lower, and Lewis Hamilton had finished fifth or lower.

This was the only combination of results which would have seen Antonelli crowned as F1's youngest-ever world champion - but his ninth victory of the season was coupled with Russell's P8 and Hamilton's P4, meaning Antonelli heads to Mexico City next week with a 123-point lead over Russell and a 124-point advantage over Hamilton.

After the Austin race, Antonelli has scored 365 points, against 242 for Russell and 241 for Hamilton.

There are 125 points remaining in the season, meaning that to keep their title hopes alive, Russell or Hamilton must win in Mexico City.

If any other driver aside from those two win in Mexico, Antonelli will be champion.

If either of them do, Antonelli would be required to take a P9 finish if Russell wins or a P10 finish if Hamilton wins.

He is still on course to shatter Sebastian Vettel's record as the youngest F1 champion, with the German 23 years, 4 months, 11 days old when he won the 2010 title.

Antonelli will now be at least 20 years, 2 months, 7 days old if he wins the title in Mexico, beating Vettel's record by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days.

title: Kimi Antonelli on verge of smashing F1 record book after sublime US GP victory
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli cruised to victory in Austin, but the title-crowning must wait until Mexico City.

25 October 10:39PM

Kimi Antonelli breezed to a comfortable victory in the United States Grand Prix but missed out on clinching the F1 drivers' title at the Circuit of the Americas.

The Italian aced the start and made a one-stop strategy work with ease, winning by a sizeable margin over Charles Leclerc in second and Max Verstappen in third.

Seven-time world champion Lewis Hamilton finished fourth, keeping the Briton mathematically in title contention. McLaren's Lando Norris finished fifth.

As George Russell finished eighth he also remains in contention, meaning Antonelli's wait to become world champion will continue until Mexico City, where wrapping up the title is all but guaranteed.

Kimi Antonelli on verge of smashing F1 record book after sublime US GP victory

# Driver Team Time Tyre

Results are being loaded...

Kimi Antonelli masters United States GP start

Starting from pole position, Kimi Antonelli knew he had his first chance to seal a maiden world title, but to do so, he had to win, with George Russell finishing ninth or lower and Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower by the chequered flag.

Interestingly, Antonelli and Russell, who started sixth on the grid, opted to start on medium tyres, while Max Verstappen in second, Isack Hadjar in third, Charles Leclerc in fourth and Lewis Hamilton in fifth went for the softs. In theory, this gave Verstappen an advantage on the run to the first corner.

As the lights went out, that did not happen. Antonelli made an excellent start to keep the lead, while a stunning move by Leclerc moved him past Verstappen at Turn 3.

Leclerc's spell in second was short-lived, as he dropped back to third by the end of the first lap. Hamilton was fourth. The leading drivers quickly settled into a rhythm, with Antonelli's advantage over Verstappen standing at just 2.5s after five laps.

Crucially, Russell was in sixth; however, he was given a five-second time penalty on lap nine for gaining an advantage by leaving the circuit on the opening lap. Nevertheless, it did not put him at risk of falling outside the top eight.

The field was clearly focused on tyre preservation in the first half of the race, as sizeable gaps appeared between the leading drivers, making for an uneventful start to the Grand Prix.

To much surprise, Red Bull and Verstappen blinked first and committed to a two-stop strategy, pitting the Dutchman at the start of lap 14. This left Mercedes with a big decision to make. Antonelli, on the medium tyres, did not pit the following lap, but Hamilton did, switching to a new set of mediums.

A lap later, Leclerc followed suit, also switching to medium tyres, as did Oscar Piastri. Verstappen cycled back ahead of Leclerc, while the Monegasque remained ahead of Hamilton. Lando Norris joined the pit-stop fun on lap 17, with both McLarens switching to hard tyres.

Mercedes continued to hold its nerve, with Verstappen and Leclerc getting back ahead of Russell on fresh tyres. It became clear that the Silver Arrows and Hadjar were sticking to a one-stop strategy. On lap 22, Russell finally pitted and also served his penalty.

© XPB Images

Kimi Antonelli one-stop proves decisive

Two laps later, Antonelli was finally brought in for hard tyres, like his team-mate, to see him through to the end of the race. The following lap, Hadjar became the final driver from the top four teams to stop.

This meant that, on lap 26, Verstappen led from Leclerc, Antonelli, Hamilton, Norris, Hadjar, Piastri and Russell. However, Verstappen was certain to stop again, while both Ferraris potentially had another stop to make.

On lap 30, Verstappen complained over the radio that his car was "undriveable", with Red Bull informing him of an engine-mapping problem. Hadjar reported a similar issue. The four-time world champion pitted for a second time a lap later, switching to medium tyres.

Verstappen's pit stop unleashed Leclerc and Antonelli, while his second stop dropped him to fifth, behind Norris in fourth. Hamilton was third. Leclerc's spell in the lead did not last long, as Antonelli breezed past at Turn 12 on lap 32 to retake the lead.

On laps 39 and 40, Ferrari joined the two-stop party. Hamilton boxed first, followed by Leclerc, with both switching to hard tyres. Leclerc and Hamilton rejoined in fourth and sixth, leaving Hadjar sandwiched between the two Ferraris. That lasted until lap 42, when the Frenchman was easily passed by Hamilton.

With 13 laps remaining, Antonelli comfortably led from Norris, who had Verstappen just one second behind in third. Leclerc and Hamilton sat fourth and fifth, both showing strong pace. With 10 laps remaining, Norris had Verstappen and Leclerc both within one second.

Norris' defence ended on lap 47, as Verstappen and Leclerc moved past before the Ferrari driver set his sights on the Red Bull. On lap 49, at Turn 12, Leclerc swooped into second, dropping Verstappen to third.

Things quickly worsened for Norris, as Hamilton made his way past. There was a brief moment of drama on lap 52, as a Virtual Safety Car was deployed after Valtteri Bottas came to a halt, but a full Safety Car was not required.

For Mercedes, it was a moment of relief, as the VSC did not prevent Antonelli from securing another easy victory and taking a big step towards becoming world champion. Leclerc and Verstappen completed the podium, with Hamilton fourth, Norris fifth and Russell eighth. Hadjar was sixth, Piastri seventh, Liam Lawson ninth and Pierre Gasly 10th. As a result, the title will likely be sealed in Mexico City.

title: When Kimi Antonelli can win the 2026 F1 drivers' world championship?
excerpt:
Check out the title permutations for when Kimi Antonelli can win the 2026 F1 drivers' world championship title and become the youngest world champion in F1 history.

When can Kimi Antonelli win the 2026 F1 drivers' championship title?

Following the 2026 United States Grand Prix, Kimi Antonelli holds a 123-point lead over Mercedes team-mate George Russell.

No other driver is within 100 points of the Italian, who is increasingly set to become the youngest F1 world champion and shatter Sebastian Vettel's record of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by over three years.

Antonelli, who turned 20 in August 2026, has dominated the season, taking a ninth win in Austin, but it was not enough to win the championship, although it is almost certain he will in Mexico City next time out.

The article continues below.

THIS ARTICLE WILL BE UPDATED FOLLOWING EVERY GRAND PRIX UNTIL ANTONELLI WINS THE 2026 F1 WORLD DRIVERS' TITLE.

How Kimi Antonelli can win the title in Mexico

After the United States Grand Prix, there are five races scheduled to take place in the season, each worth 25 points.

This gives a total of 125 points remaining in the championship, with Antonelli holding a 123-point lead over Russell and a 124-point lead over Lewis Hamilton.

For Antonelli to win the title in Mexico City the following events must happen.

Russell or Hamilton must win the grand prix. If any other driver does, Antonelli is champion.

If Russell wins, Antonelli must finish P9 or higher.

If Hamilton wins, Antonelli must finish P10 or higher.

With second place only offering 18 points, if Russell or Hamilton were to finish there in Mexico and Antonelli not score, the gap would be 105 to Russell or 106 to Hamilton - exceeding the total of 100 points which remain after Mexico, and thus sealing Antonelli's title.

Should Antonelli win the title in Mexico City, he will be 20 years, 2 months, 7 days old, beating Vettel's record by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days.

title: Lewis Hamilton makes Kimi Antonelli observation after assuming huge F1 'burden'
excerpt:
Lewis Hamilton believes Kimi Antonelli has shown he is an "old soul in a young body" at assuming the "burden" and "weight" of racing in F1.

Antonelli, then 18-years-old, was the driver chosen as the replacement for seven-time world champion Hamilton after he left Mercedes for Ferrari ahead of the 2025 season, with the Italian enduring a mixed debut season.

After finishing fourth on his Australia debut, scoring fastest lap in Japan, Sprint pole in Miami, and a first podium in Canada, Antonelli's form dipped during the summer, with the nadir coming at the Belgian GP.

Antonelli rallied in the second half of the season, before unleashing his potential in 2026, and has taken eight grand prix wins thus far, including five in a row between China and Monaco, to open up a 102-point championship lead over George Russell in the sister car.

Should Antonelli win in the United States, Russell finish ninth or lower and Hamilton fifth or lower, Antonelli will become the youngest-ever F1 champion - and the first Italian to do so since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

Reflecting on his successor and likely 36th different F1 champion, the 30th explained how Antonelli had taken everything "in his stride."

"When I was [at Mercedes], I knew who was going to be replacing me. Kimi was around the team, following us a lot, particularly in the last year that I was there," Hamilton told media, including RacingNews365.

"And I think it was the right decision to create an opportunity for a young and up-and-coming driver. Kimi had shown his abilities in the lower categories and his enthusiasm, his charm and his good approach to everything. He was always fitting really well into the environment.

"But I think he's really taken it in his stride. It's been really great to see his performances this year. It's massively impressive, and he deserves to be the champion.

"I know how amazing it is to work in that environment in the office back at the factory, with all the people, how hard everybody works and how much talent there is within that team. So, I already knew the support structure they would bring around him.

"I could assume that he was going to be fine with the burden, sorry, the weight, you have on you when you have to do all these appearances and all these things pulled left, right and centre.

"But I think he's taken it in his stride, and he's a relatively old soul in that young body, I would say."

[Article continues below].

Hamilton on Mercedes revival

Antonelli inherited Hamilton's race engineer, Peter Bonnington, when he joined Mercedes, with Hamilton-Bonnington the most successful driver-engineer pairing of all time, with 83 wins and six drivers' titles together.

Bonnington, who also worked with the other seven-time champion Michael Schumacher at Mercedes, was one of the Mercedes engineering team Hamilton also name-checked as helping Antonelli.

"Getting to work alongside Bono is such an amazing experience," said Hamilton.

"But they've got so many great people in that team, and that's the reason why they are where they are. I honestly have such admiration for what they do.

"Also, as I said, with Bono, he's amazing at really putting his arm around you and supporting you, as are [Andrew] Shovlin and Simon [Cole] and everyone in the team. I guess you never know how anyone's going to do under pressure until you see them.

"To see them back at the top is no surprise to me because I got to experience it for many, many years there.

" I think in his first year, it's tough for anybody going into a seat like that, into a team like that, and getting up and running with all the expectations on your shoulders, the things you have, the commitment you have, all those sorts of things."

title: Max Verstappen holds key advantage as Kimi Antonelli plays first championship point
excerpt:
Max Verstappen holds a potentially decisive tyre advantage for the United States Grand Prix, providing the Red Bull driver with greater strategic flexibility as Kimi Antonelli bids to secure his maiden F1 title.

Starting second behind pole-sitter Antonelli, Verstappen has two fresh sets of soft tyres available, offering an advantage off the line and during the opening stint.

Crucially, the Dutchman's allocation also allows him to switch to a two-stop strategy should degradation prove higher than anticipated.

Verstappen has one fresh set each of the hard and medium compounds, alongside two used sets of softs. Third-placed Isack Hadjar has an identical allocation.

Antonelli, meanwhile, has one fresh hard, one fresh and one used medium, and three used soft sets.

Pirelli expects a one-stop race, although the performance advantage of the soft compound could encourage Verstappen to adopt an aggressive approach.

"The C4 [soft tyre] confirmed a performance advantage over the C3 [medium tyre] in terms of both grip and lap time, a factor that ensures clear differentiation between the available options," Dario Marrafuschi, Pirelli head of motorsport, said.

"In race pace running, however, the two softer compounds proved to be very closely matched, increasing the number of strategic scenarios available to the teams.

"The simulations indicate that a one-stop strategy remains the most effective solution in terms of overall race time.

"The soft-medium combination could be chosen by more than one team in order to maximise the grip advantage offered by the red-banded tyre.

"The hard nevertheless remains a valid option for the second stint, regardless of whether the race is started on the soft or the medium."

[Article continues below]

Safety car threat or high wear could shake up United States GP strategy

An early safety car could significantly alter the strategic picture at the Circuit of the Americas, potentially encouraging teams to switch to the C2 hard compound.

Every driver has a fresh set of hards available, providing an alternative should an early neutralisation make a lengthy final stint viable.

Antonelli must win the race to stand any chance of clinching the championship, with George Russell needing to finish ninth or lower and Lewis Hamilton fifth or lower.

Russell starts sixth, one place behind Hamilton, while victory for Antonelli would eliminate Verstappen from title contention regardless of his finishing position.

However, Verstappen's additional fresh soft compound could prove particularly valuable if higher tyre wear forces teams away from the preferred one-stop strategy.

"An early neutralisation could in fact encourage teams to complete the remainder of the grand prix on the C2 [hard tyre]," Marrafuschi added, before highlighting Verstappen's key advantage.

"Should degradation prove higher than expected, a two-stop strategy based on a soft-medium-soft sequence could also become an attractive option.

"The time difference compared with the one-stop strategy remains relatively small, but track position and the potential impact of traffic must also be taken into account.

"Ultimately, it will be the evolution of track conditions and tomorrow’s temperatures that determine the choices made by the teams."

title: Sunday morning Austin weather update for F1 United States GP
excerpt:
The 2026 F1 United States Grand Prix is set to feature weather conditions which could potentially aid drivers in making overtaking moves.

The race, set for a 15:00 local time start in Texas, is set to feature winds blowing in from the south-east, which is a direct headwind into the Turn 1 braking zone.

Headwinds increase the slipstream effect, meaning a following car can use this as extra boost to overtake a rival, with Turn 1 being one of the prime overtaking spots.

The other major spot is at the end of the back straight into Turn 12, but this runs north-east to south-west, meaning there will be a crosswind under braking from left-to-right as the driver looks into the left-hander.

In terms of temperatures, the race is expected to be run in the high 20-degree Celsius mark, possibly dipping into the low 30s.

Rain is not forecast, with the nearest current rain cells being to the north-north-west of Texas, with a system in the Rocky Mountains, but it will not travel to Austin to impact the 56-lap Grand Prix where Kimi Antonelli can become the youngest F1 world champion if he wins from pole position.

title: Isack Hadjar explains 'gutted' emotion despite Austin 'disaster' recovery
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has explained why he felt "gutted" following United States Grand Prix qualifying, despite a strong recovery to third after a "disaster" of a weekend.

Throughout practice, Hadjar struggled for balance and comfort in his RB22 machine, and was well off the pace of Max Verstappen on Friday.

However, in qualifying, Hadjar rallied and was able to secure third on the grid, just 0.036s down on Verstappen, with both drivers setting their fastest laps on their first Q3 runs.

It is the best two-car qualifying result for Red Bull in the season, although Hadjar did take third on the road in Malaysia before a five-place penalty for a new ICE component, which dropped him to eighth.

Analysing his remarkable turnaround, the Frenchman described why he was feeling "gutted" at potentially throwing away a chance at a first F1 pole position - with Kimi Antonelli only 0.215s quicker.

"I mean, it's been a disaster of a weekend for me. I've had all my lap times deleted all the time," Hadjar reflected.

"[In Free Practice 3], I could not complete a single lap on the soft tyres, but I knew there was something in the car because there were times when I could do half a lap and I felt comfortable, but I could never finish it.

"But in qualifying, the car really came alive a bit more for me. We really dug deep on the set-up. We tried so many things this weekend, and it really paid off.

"So, on that note, it's really, really satisfying. But I'm a bit gutted, not too much about the last lap, but more about the first attempt in Q3, because yes, the track was worse on that final lap and it wasn’t a great lap, but it was the same for everyone.

"On that first lap, I really felt like I lost so much time with that massive tailwind I got, and I felt like there was a bit more, but I am happy with the comeback, and I thought we had a shot at the front row."

[Article continues below].

Hadjar's victory chances

Turning to the race with two Red Bulls against the lone Mercedes of Antonelli, Hadjar was optimistic about strategy coming into play.

"Yeah, I mean, it's the two of us, so it's a bit of an advantage, so we'll try and use that," he said when asked if Red Bull could challenge for the win.
